# SK2140 — The override declares a parameter default or `params` the call site will not use

<!-- Generated from Rules/Rikarin.Skala.Rules.Metadata/rules.json. Do not edit. -->

An override or an implicit interface implementation declares a different default value, or a different `params` modifier, than the member it overrides or implements.

| | |
|---|---|
| Category | Correctness |
| Default severity | warning |
| Scope | Semantic |
| Needs a compilation | yes |
| Fix | yes, review it |
| Language version floor | — |
| Since | 2.0 |

## Why

A default value is not part of the call — it is baked into the call site at compile time, from the *static* type of the receiver. Through a base-class or interface reference the base's default is the one that is written into the IL, and the override's is dead text; through the derived type the override's wins. The same member therefore behaves as two different methods depending on which reference the caller happens to hold, and nothing in either declaration says so. ⚠ **`params` behaves differently from a default and the difference was measured rather than assumed.** An *override* does not get to change it at all: `params` dropped on an override still expands through the derived type, and `params` added on an override whose base has none expands through neither reference — both call sites were compiled and both answers read off the build. Expansion is decided by the base, always, so an override's own `params` keyword is dead text in both directions and there is nothing to report. An *interface implementation* is the opposite: it inherits nothing, so an implementation that drops the interface's `params` gives `((IPlain)x).Accept("a", 1, 2)` compiling and `x.Accept("a", 1, 2)` failing with `CS1501`, from one object. That asymmetry is the finding. ⚠ **The compiler is silent on every one of these.** It emits `CS1066` when an *explicit* interface implementation carries a default, because such a member can never be called with optional arguments at all — that case is hosted and this rule declines it. For an override, and for an implicit interface implementation, there is no diagnostic at any warning level; the shape was compiled and the build read, not assumed.

## Example

Instead of:

```csharp
class Base {
    public virtual void Write(string text, bool flush = false) { }
}

class Derived : Base {
    public override void Write(string text, bool flush = true) { }
}
```

Write:

```csharp
class Base {
    public virtual void Write(string text, bool flush = false) { }
}

class Derived : Base {
    public override void Write(string text, bool flush = false) { }
}
```

## When it does not fire

⚠ **Explicit interface implementations are declined, because `CS1066` already reports them** and ADR-008's answer to a diagnostic the compiler ships is to let it do the work. ⚠ **The base is the one the declaration actually names.** For an `override` that is `OverriddenMethod`; for an implicit interface implementation it is the interface member `FindImplementationForInterfaceMember` maps back to this one, and a member that implements several interface members with conflicting defaults is declined outright rather than reported against an arbitrary one of them — there is no single value to align to and a fix would have to pick. ⚠ **The whole declaration is one finding with one edit, and that is a correctness constraint rather than tidiness.** C# requires optional parameters to form a suffix, so deleting one redundant default out of two leaves `(int a = 1, int b)`, which is `CS1737` — `skala fix` applies one finding at a time, and per-parameter findings would break the build on the tool's own advice between the first edit and the second. A parameter whose default the base also declares, with the same value, is not reported; equality is on the constant, so `0` against `0` is a match and `0` against `0.0` is not — the mismatch direction is the safe one to get wrong. ⚠ **A `params` mismatch on an override is declined by construction rather than by a guard**, which is why no filter for it appears anywhere: Roslyn propagates the base's `params` onto the override's parameter symbol, so `IsParams` is equal on both sides even where no keyword is written and the comparison cannot fire. That is the correct answer for the reason the rationale gives, and it means the `params` half of this rule only ever reports interface implementations. Partial and abstract declarations have no override to compare against and are silent, as is generated code.

## Configuration

- `dotnet_diagnostic.SK2140.severity`
